coachingPoints: Install one clear pace identity in preseason — do not waffle between fast and slow.
Use the 'eight-second rule' aggressively: cross half-court in under five seconds on makes and misses.
Chart possessions per game and points per possession, not just total points.
Practice the same late-game sets until players can run them without thinking.
commonMistakes: Playing fast without a plan — speed without spacing is just chaos.
Holding the ball with no advantage and letting the defense rest.
Ignoring the score and foul situation in the final two minutes.
Calling timeout when the team has momentum instead of letting them play.
description: Pace, rhythm and game management — how tempo shapes offense and defense and how to control it.
gameSituations: After a made basket — push immediately while the defense is jogging back.
Against a superior team — slow the game, limit possessions, make each one count.
Protecting a lead — use the full clock, attack late, no quick threes.
Chasing a lead — speed up, foul strategically, extend the game with timeouts.

howTo.detail: Pace is measured in possessions per game. Fast teams push after every rebound and made basket, attacking before the defense sets. Slow teams walk the ball up, run the clock, and value each possession.
howTo.title: Choose your pace

howTo.detail: The first six to eight seconds after a change of possession are the most efficient scoring window in basketball. Sprint the floor, run wide lanes, and look for the early drag screen or pitch-ahead pass.
howTo.title: Attack in early offense

howTo.detail: Against a set defense, run your actions with purpose: one screen, one cut, one read — then the next. Standing around 'running clock' with no action lets the defense rest.
howTo.title: Execute in the half court

howTo.detail: The score, the foul count, and the time remaining should change your decisions. Up five with two minutes left? Use clock, attack the paint, no fouls. Down eight? Speed up and take quick threes.
howTo.title: Let the game situation decide

howTo.detail: Coaches change tempo with substitutions (fresh legs run faster), timeouts (kill the opponent's run), and play calls (push or slow). Players change tempo with their first three steps after every rebound.
howTo.title: Control tempo deliberately

title: Game Flow & Tempo
whatIsIt: Tempo is the speed at which a game is played — how quickly teams move from defense to offense and how fast they attack once they have the ball. Some teams sprint at every opportunity; others walk the ball up and squeeze the shot clock. Neither style is automatically better; the right tempo is the one that suits your roster and exploits the opponent.

Game flow is how that tempo feels moment to moment: runs of momentum, lulls, foul trouble, timeouts, and the tension of the final minutes. Teams that read the flow adjust — they push when the opponent is tired, slow down when the game gets chaotic, and manage the clock when the score demands it.
whyItMatters: Tempo is a weapon. A fast team facing a bigger opponent runs them into exhaustion; a disciplined team facing a chaotic opponent slows the game and makes every possession count. Players who understand flow make better decisions — they know when to push, when to pull back, and how the scoreboard should change their choices.
